4	Recursive generation can be modeled as iterative density estimation: each depth-$k$ model approximates the distribution of $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$, which was itself sampled from the depth-$(k{-}1)$ model.
5	\citet{shumailov2024_nature} show that this process contracts the support of the learned distribution, with low-probability tokens lost first.
6	If $p_k$ denotes the token distribution at depth $k$, the tail mass $P_k(\mathrm{ppl} > t)$ decreases monotonically in $k$ for large $t$.
7	This tail erosion predicts \texttt{p90\_ppl} as a depth marker: the 90th-percentile perplexity captures exactly the region where successive generations remove probability mass.
8	Our data confirm this prediction: \texttt{p90\_ppl} ranks top-2 in all 9 cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}), and fine-tuning loss decreases monotonically with depth for all three families.
9	Surprisal variance captures the complementary signal of distributional narrowing: as the support contracts, per-token surprise becomes more predictable.
10	
11	\paragraph{EDD upper bound.}
12	\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterize model collapse via exponential tail decay: tail mass at depth $k$ scales as $\alpha^k$ for a contraction factor $\alpha \in (0,1)$ that depends on model capacity and data size.
13	Since the dominant features track tail mass and tail mass contracts geometrically, the pairwise AUC-excess should contract at a comparable rate; EDD reaches its upper bound when adjacent-depth feature distance falls below the classifier's resolution.
14	Our empirical AUC-excess contraction (ratio 0.80 at d1v2$\to$d2v3, 0.69 at d3v4$\to$d4v5; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) is consistent with geometric decay but with a decreasing ratio, as the distribution approaches a fixed point where residual variation falls below the feature resolution.

17	\paragraph{Scale-dependent attenuation.}
18	The contraction factor $\alpha$ depends on model capacity: larger models approximate the training distribution more faithfully per step, so the per-step distributional shift is smaller ($\alpha$ closer to 1).

\subsection{Theoretical Grounding}
\label{sec:method:theory}

Recursive generation can be modeled as iterative density estimation: each depth-$k$ model approximates the distribution of $\mathcal{D}_{k-1}$, which was itself sampled from the depth-$(k{-}1)$ model.
\citet{shumailov2024_nature} show that this process contracts the support of the learned distribution, with low-probability tokens lost first.
If $p_k$ denotes the token distribution at depth $k$, the tail mass $P_k(\mathrm{ppl} > t)$ decreases monotonically in $k$ for large $t$.
This tail erosion predicts \texttt{p90\_ppl} as a depth marker: the 90th-percentile perplexity captures exactly the region where successive generations remove probability mass.
Our data confirm this prediction: \texttt{p90\_ppl} ranks top-2 in all 9 cells (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features}), and fine-tuning loss decreases monotonically with depth for all three families.
Surprisal variance captures the complementary signal of distributional narrowing: as the support contracts, per-token surprise becomes more predictable.

\paragraph{EDD upper bound.}
\citet{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} characterize model collapse via exponential tail decay: tail mass at depth $k$ scales as $\alpha^k$ for a contraction factor $\alpha \in (0,1)$ that depends on model capacity and data size.
Since the dominant features track tail mass and tail mass contracts geometrically, the pairwise AUC-excess should contract at a comparable rate; EDD reaches its upper bound when adjacent-depth feature distance falls below the classifier's resolution.
Our empirical AUC-excess contraction (ratio 0.80 at d1v2$\to$d2v3, 0.69 at d3v4$\to$d4v5; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}) is consistent with geometric decay but with a decreasing ratio, as the distribution approaches a fixed point where residual variation falls below the feature resolution.
5-class extensions to d4 for all three families (71--80\% accuracy, chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}) confirm that depth~4 remains discriminable in the multi-class setting; mean perplexity saturates before tail statistics at this depth, and the saturation of aggregate statistics places a physical ceiling on discriminability.

\paragraph{Scale-dependent attenuation.}
The contraction factor $\alpha$ depends on model capacity: larger models approximate the training distribution more faithfully per step, so the per-step distributional shift is smaller ($\alpha$ closer to 1).
EDD should therefore decrease with generator scale, since the feature distance between adjacent depths shrinks below classifier resolution at shallower depths.
Qwen2.5-14B confirms this: d0-vs-d1 AUC drops to 0.643 (vs.\ ${>}0.99$ at 1--1.5B), while d1--d3 pairwise AUCs remain above 0.70 (\S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}), consistent with the first recursive step at higher capacity: the 14B model produces a near-faithful copy of its training distribution, and the residual distributional shift is detectable only through higher-order feature statistics.

\paragraph{Strategy-dependent convergence.}
The contraction rate $\alpha$ varies with decoding strategy.
Temperature scaling ($\tau < 1$) sharpens the logit distribution uniformly and accelerates convergence to the mode; temperature depth-$d$ text should therefore resemble nucleus depth-$(d{+}1)$ text in tail statistics.
GPT-2~XL confirms this: temperature d1 median \texttt{p90\_ppl} (92.2) matches the nucleus d2 median (92.3, IQR 75.8--112.5).
Top-$k$ truncation removes the low-probability tokens that carry depth signal, predicting weaker discriminability; top-$k$ cells yield the lowest accuracy (68.9--75.8\%) across the atlas (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).

1	\section{The Depth Degradation Atlas}
2	\label{sec:atlas}
3	
4	We present the Depth Degradation Atlas: a systematic empirical map of how statistical fingerprints evolve across recursive generation depths, models, and decoding strategies.
5	The atlas spans $3 \times 3 = 9$ model--strategy cells evaluated at depths $d \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$, with depth extensions to $d{=}5$ for cross-model EDD validation (\S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}).
6	
7	%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
8	\subsection{In-Distribution Performance}
9	\label{sec:atlas:id}
10	
11	Table~\ref{tab:main_matrix} reports four-class Random Forest accuracy (5-fold CV, 200 trees) across all nine cells.
12	Accuracy ranges from 68.9\% (Pythia, top-$k$) to 85.9\% (GPT-2~XL, temperature), all exceeding the 25\% chance baseline by a wide margin.
13	Two axis effects emerge.
14	GPT-2~XL achieves the highest accuracy under every strategy (75.8--85.9\%), followed by OLMo (74.4--82.3\%) and Pythia (68.9--78.7\%).
15	Top-$k$ sampling yields the lowest accuracy in every model.
16	The mean within-model strategy gap is 9.3~pp, comparable to the 7.2~pp mean within-strategy model gap; decoding strategy and model family contribute roughly equally to performance variance.
17	
18	\begin{table}[t]
19	\centering
20	\small
21	\caption{Four-class RF accuracy (\%) with bootstrap 95\% CI (${\pm}$half-width; $B{=}1{,}000$). RF with 200 trees, evaluated via 5-fold stratified CV (seed=42). Parenthesized: d1--d3 balanced accuracy from the same 4-class RF (chance = 25\% / 33\%). Depth-0 recall exceeds 97\% in all cells. Within-distribution ordinal quality: MAE\,=\,0.23, QWK\,=\,0.89 (QWK$_{\text{d1--d3}}$\,=\,0.74); 98.2\% of errors fall on adjacent depths ($|\Delta| \leq 1$).}
22	\label{tab:main_matrix}
23	\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
24	\toprule
25	& Nucleus & Temp.\ $\tau{=}0.9$ & Top-$k$ \\
26	\midrule
27	Pythia-1.4B  & 78.7{\scriptsize$\pm$0.6}\,(71.8) & 76.8{\scriptsize$\pm$0.6}\,(69.3) & 68.9{\scriptsize$\pm$0.6}\,(58.9) \\
28	OLMo-1B     & 78.9{\scriptsize$\pm$0.6}\,(72.7) & 82.3{\scriptsize$\pm$0.5}\,(76.6) & 74.4{\scriptsize$\pm$0.6}\,(66.2) \\
29	GPT-2~XL    & \textbf{84.3}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.5}\,(79.6) & \textbf{85.9}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.4}\,(81.5) & \textbf{75.8}{\scriptsize$\pm$0.6}\,(68.1) \\
30	\bottomrule
31	\end{tabular}
32	\end{table}
33	
34	\paragraph{Per-class recall.}
35	Depth-0 recall exceeds 97\% in all 9 cells.
36	Among generated depths, d2 consistently yields the lowest recall (44--73\%), followed by d3 (61--80\%) and d1 (72--91\%).
37	The d2 trough reflects its position at the center of the depth gradient, where features overlap with both d1 and d3, consistent with d2-vs-d3 as the EDD bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}).
38	Full per-class recall appears in Appendix~\ref{app:per_class}.
39	
40	%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
41	\subsection{Feature Consistency Across the Grid}
42	\label{sec:atlas:features}
43	
44	Despite the 17.1~pp accuracy spread across cells, a small feature family dominates in every setting.
45	Perplexity tail statistics as a feature group dominate depth discrimination: the 90th-percentile perplexity (\texttt{p90\_ppl}) ranks top-2 by Gini importance in all 9 cells; surprisal variance (\texttt{var\_surprisal}) in 8/9 under SHAP (7/9 under Gini; Appendix~\ref{app:permutation}).\footnote{Individual feature rankings should be interpreted cautiously given high multicollinearity (VIF${>}$10 for 14--16/19 features); the group-level dominance of perplexity tail statistics is robust across importance measures.}
46	Table~\ref{tab:feature_importance} shows the full per-cell ranking.
47	
48	Cross-model feature-rank Spearman correlation averages $\bar{\rho} = 0.868$ (range $[0.619, 0.954]$): models agree on which features carry depth information even when they differ in absolute accuracy.
49	Among strategies, top-$k$ yields the highest cross-model rank correlation ($\rho = 0.811$): the deterministic vocabulary truncation imposes a more uniform feature landscape across architectures, at the cost of weaker overall signal (\S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}).
50	
51	Feature ablation confirms this concentration: the top-5 features achieve 97.6\% of full accuracy (76.5\% vs.\ 78.4\%), with perplexity statistics alone reaching 76.6\% (vs.\ surprisal 73.2\%, other categories ${\leq}$47\%).
52	
53	The feature hierarchy shifts with depth.
54	At shallow boundaries (d1 vs.\ d2), \texttt{var\_surprisal} dominates importance; at deeper boundaries (d3 vs.\ d4, d4 vs.\ d5), tail perplexity statistics (\texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{kurtosis\_ppl}) take over.
55	This transition aligns with model-collapse dynamics~\cite{shumailov2024_nature}: early recursion narrows the surprisal distribution (captured by its variance), while later steps erode the perplexity tail (captured by upper quantiles and kurtosis).

84	\label{fig:atlas_heatmap}
85	\end{figure}
86	
87	%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
88	\subsection{Monotonicity and Inter-Depth Distances}
89	\label{sec:atlas:monotonicity}
90	
91	Depth features exhibit strong monotonic trends: perplexity tail statistics (\texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{mean\_surprisal}) decrease with depth (Spearman $\rho = -1.0$ across cell-level medians) while repetition features increase. This pattern reflects the complementary narrowing and self-repetition of distribution collapse.
92	Inter-depth distances are non-uniform: d0-vs-d1 AUC exceeds 0.99 in all 9 cells, whereas d2-vs-d3 ranges from 0.69 to 0.89; separating adjacent deep generations requires the tail statistics identified in \S\ref{sec:atlas:features}.
93	
94	\begin{figure}[t]
95	\centering
96	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_feature_trajectory.pdf}
97	\caption{Feature trajectories across depths $d{=}0$ to $d{=}3$, stratified by model (columns) and strategy (line style). Top row: \texttt{p90\_ppl} (monotonically decreasing). Middle: \texttt{var\_surprisal} (decreasing). Bottom: \texttt{rep\_3gram} (increasing). Shaded bands: interquartile range. The $d{=}0 \to d{=}1$ gap exceeds all subsequent inter-depth gaps.}
98	\label{fig:feature_trajectory}
99	\end{figure}
100	
101	%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
102	\subsection{EDD Analysis}
103	\label{sec:atlas:edd}
104	
105	We extend the benchmark to depth $d{=}5$ for all three models under nucleus sampling.
106	Each model's depth-3 LoRA checkpoint is used to finetune and generate depth-4 data, and the process repeats for depth~5; feature extraction uses the same reference model (Pythia-1.4B).
107	We train dedicated binary RF classifiers (500 trees) for each adjacent pair, as defined in Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}.
108	
109	\paragraph{AUC decay and cross-model convergence.}
110	Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} plots the pairwise AUC decay curves.
111	For Pythia-1.4B (nucleus), AUC decays monotonically from $0.999$ (d0v1) to $0.683$ (d4v5); the steepest drop is d1v2$\to$d2v3.
112	The AUC-excess ($\mathrm{AUC} - 0.5$) contraction ratio decreases from 0.80 (d1v2$\to$d2v3) to 0.69 (d3v4$\to$d4v5); convergence toward indistinguishability accelerates with depth.
113	The d3-vs-d4 AUC clusters near $T{=}0.75$ for all three models (Pythia $0.784$, OLMo $0.765$, GPT-2~XL $0.750$), while d4-vs-d5 uniformly falls below $0.70$.
114	Bootstrap testing ($H_0{:}\, \mathrm{AUC} \leq 0.75$) yields $p = 0.001$ for Pythia, $p = 0.091$ for OLMo, and $p = 0.505$ for GPT-2~XL; a depth-4 decay boundary emerges with graded confidence.
115	
116	\paragraph{EDD threshold sensitivity.}

144	\label{sec:atlas:strategy}
145	
146	The three strategies induce qualitatively distinct degradation trajectories.
147	Temperature ($\tau{=}0.9$) yields the highest accuracy in 2/3 models (GPT-2~XL 85.9\%, OLMo 82.3\%) because uniform logit scaling accelerates convergence to an attractor~\cite{shumailov2024_nature}, amplifying the fingerprint but creating a boundary reversal risk under cross-strategy transfer (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).

As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises, yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical; it is already occurring in the wild. Yet whether the recursive generation depth of a text can be estimated from its statistical properties remains unstudied, a question that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.

We find that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are \textbf{consistent in direction but scale-dependent in magnitude} across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics (the 90th-percentile perplexity, \texttt{p90\_ppl}, and surprisal variance, \texttt{var\_surprisal}) emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.
Instruction-tuned variants exhibit monotonically decreasing AUC (regularization), whereas base models can show non-monotonic trajectories; instruction tuning thus acts as a regularizer on the depth signal rather than a source of degradation.

This paper is an empirical study and problem formalization rather than an algorithmic contribution.
We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and introduce a lightweight pipeline: compute 19 reference-model statistical features (effective dimensionality ${\approx}$4--5 due to multicollinearity; \S\ref{sec:atlas:features}) and classify with a Random Forest into $K{+}1$ depth classes.
To characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families $\times$ decoding strategies spanning 4 depths (180K samples).
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formalization and benchmark.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, introduce the EDD metric, and construct a 180K-sample benchmark ($3$ model families $\times$ $3$ decoding strategies $\times$ $4$ depths).

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} Perplexity tail statistics dominate depth discrimination (top-2 in 9/9 and 8/9 cells); $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}4$ for all three families, validated by 5-class (d0--d4) extension on three families (71--80\%); at the stricter $T{=}0.75$, Pythia achieves $p{=}0.001$ with graded confidence across families in the d3--d4 region.

    \item \textbf{Generalization and cross-strategy analysis.} Cross-model LOO 66.4\% (d1--d3: 55.4\%), cross-seed replication across three families, prompted 69.5\%, cross-scale 7--14B (54--70\%, attenuating with scale), cross-domain arXiv 74.1\%. Cross-strategy transfer (59.1\%) reveals a structural difficulty: different decoding strategies induce qualitatively distinct degradation trajectories, with d1/d2 boundary inversion under strategy mismatch. Surface-text controls (zero-shot LLMs 30--36\%) and binary detection/membership inference baselines (DetectGPT, Min-K\% Prob: 30--33\%) confirm the signal resides in distributional statistics inaccessible from surface text or detection scores.
\end{itemize}

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}
5	Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.
6	Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion under logistic regression (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments ($\Delta < 0.02$\,pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$); a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is therefore needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.
7	
8	\paragraph{Strategy-unknown deployment.}
9	In strategy-unknown settings, naive transfer on d1--d3 yields only 45.9\%, and d1/d2 predictions may invert.
10	A two-stage pipeline recovers 11.5\,pp over LOO, though per-model gains vary (GPT-2~XL $+$16.4\,pp vs.\ Pythia $+$8.0\,pp).
11	Practical deployment requires either strategy metadata or learned routing.
12	
13	\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
14	Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$97\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.
15	Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).
16	
17	\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
18	The primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled LoRA fine-tuning (1--1.5B models), a design that isolates the depth variable but diverges from wild contamination where models train on mixed corpora with prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions.
19	Domain bias controls confirm depth as the dominant factor: LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
20	Cross-scale experiments (7--14B, \S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) show signal that attenuates with scale; at 14B, d0/d1 separability nearly vanishes ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}0$) while d1--d3 discrimination persists; this constitutes a boundary condition for the current feature set (confounded by self-reference model; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_confounds}).
21	A base-model control suggests instruction-tuning regularizes degradation.
22	Segment-level estimation in mixed-depth documents remains open (Appendix~\ref{app:mixed_depth}); in particular, partial mixing (accumulation), where a single document contains fragments from different recursive depths, is a key open question, as our framework assumes uniform depth per passage.
23	
24	\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}
25	On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), per-model FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL).
26	A pooled RF classifier evaluated on larger corpora (10{,}000 passages each) yields 34\% FPR on C4 and 17\% on FineWeb \cite{penedo2024_fineweb}; the gap reflects quality filtering in FineWeb removing feature-anomalous text that triggers false positives.
27	Misclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\texttt{rep\_3gram} $+$37\%, \texttt{rep\_4gram} $+$75\% vs.\ correctly classified d0).
28	Confidence thresholding ($P(\mathrm{d0}) \geq 0.15$) reduces pooled FPR from 34\%/17\% to 2.8\%/0.7\% on C4/FineWeb at minimal accuracy cost ($-$0.3\,pp); high FPR is therefore a decision-threshold problem, not a fundamental calibration defect, though the optimal threshold remains domain-dependent (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).
29	
30	\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
31	Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.
32	
33	\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}
34	Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically, as observed in all our configurations.
35	However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
36	Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
37	In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
38	The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.
39	
40	\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
41	Reference model choice affects classification accuracy by up to 11\,pp; same-family references yield optimal performance, though all configurations exceed $2.5\times$ chance.
42	Surprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators.
43	For the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2~XL measurements are cross-model.
44	Empirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.7\% vs.\ GPT-2~XL 85.9\%); the overlap therefore does not confer a systematic advantage.
45	An ablation with OLMo-1B and GPT-2 XL as alternative references shows accuracy ranging from 67--79\% across three reference architectures (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}), all exceeding $2.5\times$ chance; same-family reference yields optimal performance ($\Delta{\leq}$11\,pp).
46	The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.
47	Reference-free surface features alone achieve 53.7\% (partial signal in lexical statistics) but trail the full pipeline by 25pp; surprisal-based features are therefore essential.
48	Simple multi-reference ensembling does not outperform the best single reference (73.7\% vs.\ 78.6\%).
49	
50	\paragraph{Single LoRA instance.}
51	Cross-seed replication covers 3 of 9 cells (Pythia, OLMo, GPT-2~XL nucleus); seed=43 yields $+$0.1 to $+$3.2\,pp higher accuracy, with 2/3 deltas statistically significant (non-overlapping CIs).
52	Feature rankings and depth ordering are consistent across seeds, but single-seed absolute accuracy carries ${\sim}$1--3\,pp uncertainty; cross-cell comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.
53	
54	\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
55	Depth signal scales with passage length (68.4\% at 128 tokens, 77.8\% at 512; Appendix~\ref{app:length_ablation}), saturating near 500 tokens.
56	Prompted generation was validated on only 1 of 9 cells (GPT-2~XL nucleus); generalization to other model--strategy configurations under prompted conditions is not established.
57	Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and curated synthetic data may not trigger collapse \cite{falahati2026_curated}, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.
58	
59	\section*{Ethics Statement}
60	
61	This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
62	No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
63	Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
64	Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
65	This research used AI coding assistants for experiment implementation and writing drafts.
66	All scientific decisions, experimental design, and result interpretation were conducted by the authors.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}
Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.
Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion under logistic regression (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments ($\Delta < 0.02$\,pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$); a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is therefore needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.

\paragraph{Strategy-unknown deployment.}
In strategy-unknown settings, naive transfer on d1--d3 yields only 45.9\%, and d1/d2 predictions may invert.
A two-stage pipeline recovers 11.5\,pp over LOO, though per-model gains vary (GPT-2~XL $+$16.4\,pp vs.\ Pythia $+$8.0\,pp).
Practical deployment requires either strategy metadata or learned routing.

\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$97\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.
Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).

\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
The primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled LoRA fine-tuning (1--1.5B models), a design that isolates the depth variable but diverges from wild contamination where models train on mixed corpora with prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions.
Domain bias controls confirm depth as the dominant factor: LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
Cross-scale experiments (7--14B, \S\ref{sec:gen:crossscale}) show signal that attenuates with scale; at 14B, d0/d1 separability nearly vanishes ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}0$) while d1--d3 discrimination persists; this constitutes a boundary condition for the current feature set (confounded by self-reference model; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_confounds}).
A base-model control suggests instruction-tuning regularizes degradation.
Segment-level estimation in mixed-depth documents remains open (Appendix~\ref{app:mixed_depth}); in particular, partial mixing (accumulation), where a single document contains fragments from different recursive depths, is a key open question, as our framework assumes uniform depth per passage.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}
On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), per-model FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL).

Misclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\texttt{rep\_3gram} $+$37\%, \texttt{rep\_4gram} $+$75\% vs.\ correctly classified d0).
Confidence thresholding ($P(\mathrm{d0}) \geq 0.15$) reduces pooled FPR from 34\%/17\% to 2.8\%/0.7\% on C4/FineWeb at minimal accuracy cost ($-$0.3\,pp); high FPR is therefore a decision-threshold problem, not a fundamental calibration defect, though the optimal threshold remains domain-dependent (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.

\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}
Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically, as observed in all our configurations.
However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.

\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
Reference model choice affects classification accuracy by up to 11\,pp; same-family references yield optimal performance, though all configurations exceed $2.5\times$ chance.
Surprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators.
For the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2~XL measurements are cross-model.
Empirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.7\% vs.\ GPT-2~XL 85.9\%); the overlap therefore does not confer a systematic advantage.
An ablation with OLMo-1B and GPT-2 XL as alternative references shows accuracy ranging from 67--79\% across three reference architectures (Appendix~\ref{app:ref_ablation}), all exceeding $2.5\times$ chance; same-family reference yields optimal performance ($\Delta{\leq}$11\,pp).

Reference-free surface features alone achieve 53.7\% (partial signal in lexical statistics) but trail the full pipeline by 25pp; surprisal-based features are therefore essential.
Simple multi-reference ensembling does not outperform the best single reference (73.7\% vs.\ 78.6\%).

\paragraph{Single LoRA instance.}
Cross-seed replication covers 3 of 9 cells (Pythia, OLMo, GPT-2~XL nucleus); seed=43 yields $+$0.1 to $+$3.2\,pp higher accuracy, with 2/3 deltas statistically significant (non-overlapping CIs).
Feature rankings and depth ordering are consistent across seeds, but single-seed absolute accuracy carries ${\sim}$1--3\,pp uncertainty; cross-cell comparisons should be interpreted cautiously.

\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
Depth signal scales with passage length (68.4\% at 128 tokens, 77.8\% at 512; Appendix~\ref{app:length_ablation}), saturating near 500 tokens.
Prompted generation was validated on only 1 of 9 cells (GPT-2~XL nucleus); generalization to other model--strategy configurations under prompted conditions is not established.
Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}, and curated synthetic data may not trigger collapse \cite{falahati2026_curated}, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.
This research used AI coding assistants for experiment implementation and writing drafts.
All scientific decisions, experimental design, and result interpretation were conducted by the authors.

1	\section{Generalization and Robustness}
2	\label{sec:generalization}
3	
4	We test whether atlas accuracy (68.9--85.9\%) reflects genuine statistical regularities across eight generalization axes (five below, three in Appendix).
5	
6	\subsection{Classifier Comparison and Surface-Text Ablation}
7	\label{sec:gen:baselines}
8	
9	Table~\ref{tab:baselines} compares ordinal depth estimation methods across all 9 atlas cells.
10	RF, XGBoost, and LightGBM on the same 19 features converge within 0.4\,pp per cell, confirming a feature-determined ceiling; on Pythia nucleus, CORAL \cite{coral2020} (78.1\%) and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} (78.2\%) match RF within 0.6\,pp ($p>0.05$).
11	
12	\paragraph{Binary detectors and membership inference.}
13	Four methods designed for binary AI-text detection or membership inference, when calibrated for ordinal depth, all fall 43--48\,pp below RF (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).
14	Min-K\% Prob \cite{shi2024_minkprob} (33.2\%) outperforms DetectGPT \cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} (30.7\%) by 2.5\,pp, consistent with token-level log-probabilities encoding more depth information than perturbation-based curvature; both remain near chance.
15	CORAL ordinal calibration does not close the gap (Min-K\% CORAL d1--d3 BalAcc: 40.4\% vs.\ RF 71.6\%), confirming that the bottleneck is input signal, not calibration.
16	Binary detector scores (Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT) repurposed as RF features reach 74.2\% on a single cell but average only 30--35\% across 9 cells (Appendix~\ref{app:detector_baselines}).
17	Adding Min-K\% probability as a 20th RF feature yields +0.48\,pp (78.4\%$\to$78.9\%); Min-K\% ranks \#3 by importance (0.095), below \texttt{p90\_ppl} (0.161) and \texttt{var\_surprisal} (0.126), while DetectGPT contributes negligibly (\#17, 0.026).
18	The gain is consistent across 8 of 9 cells but small, confirming that the 19 statistical features already capture the dominant ordinal signal.
19	
20	\paragraph{Surface-text ablation.}
21	Single-feature regression on mean perplexity performs at chance (25.1\%); zero-shot LLMs (DeepSeek V3.2, 36.2\%; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, 30.4\%) also fail (43\,pp below the best RF cell; Appendix~\ref{app:zeroshot_prompt}); depth signal resides in distributional statistics inaccessible from surface text.
22	
23	\begin{table}[t]
24	\centering
25	\small
26	\caption{Ordinal depth estimation: method comparison (mean across 9 atlas cells). Chance = 25\% (4-class) / 33.3\% (d1--d3). Min-K\%: $K{=}20$, CORAL calibration. DetectGPT: gpt2-large scoring, t5-large perturbation ($n{=}5$). 5-fold CV; SD $\leq$ 0.9\,pp for feature-based methods.}
27	\label{tab:baselines}
28	\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
29	\toprule
30	Method & 4-Cl Acc (\%) & d1--d3 BalAcc (\%) \\
31	\midrule
32	RF 19-feature (ours) & \textbf{78.4} & \textbf{71.6} \\
33	\midrule
34	Zero-shot LLM (best) & 36.2 & --- \\
35	Min-K\% Prob (CORAL) & 33.2 & 40.4 \\
36	DetectGPT (perturbation) & 30.7 & 24.3 \\
37	Random & 25.0 & 33.3 \\
38	\bottomrule
39	\end{tabular}
40	\end{table}
41	
42	Convergence confirms the signal resides in the features (three classifiers match within 0.8\,pp under cross-model transfer; Appendix~\ref{app:learned_estimator}).
43	Perplexity features alone recover 66.0\% ($-$0.5\,pp vs.\ full), while repetition/diversity features alone fall 13.6\,pp below; perplexity degradation is the dominant depth marker.
44	Raw perplexity alone performs at chance (25.1\%); the strongest single feature (\texttt{p90\_ppl}) reaches 58.3\% ($-$8.3\,pp vs.\ full); multi-dimensional characterization is required. Figure~\ref{fig:confusion_matrix} shows d0 near-perfectly identified; errors concentrate at d2/d3 in-distribution and spread to d1--d3 under transfer (RF seed std $= 0.06$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:rf_seed}).
45	Cross-seed replication across all three model families confirms consistent feature rankings and depth ordering; absolute accuracy varies by $+$0.1 to $+$3.2\,pp (same direction), with 2/3 deltas statistically significant (Appendix~\ref{app:seed_replication}).
46	
47	\begin{figure}[t]
48	\centering
49	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_confusion_matrix.pdf}
50	\caption{Confusion matrices for the best in-distribution setting (GPT-2 XL, temp $\tau{=}0.9$, 85.9\%) and the best cross-model leave-one-out transfer (OLMo holdout, 69.2\%). d0 recall exceeds 99\% in both; errors spread across the d1--d3 range under transfer.}
51	\label{fig:confusion_matrix}
52	\end{figure}
53	
54	\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
55	\label{sec:gen:crossmodel}
56	
57	We perform leave-one-model-family-out evaluation: train on two families (nucleus only), test on the held-out third (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).
58	
59	\begin{table}[t]
60	\centering
61	\small
62	\caption{Cross-model transfer (leave-one-out, nucleus only). Chance = 25\% / 33\% (d1--d3). d1--d3 bal.\ acc: Pythia 49.9\%, OLMo 59.2\%, GPT-2~XL 57.2\% (mean 55.4\%). Ordinal quality: MAE\,=\,0.39, QWK\,=\,0.81 (QWK$_{\text{d1--d3}}$\,=\,0.53); 94.8\% of errors at $|\Delta| \leq 1$.}
63	\label{tab:cross_model}
64	\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
65	\toprule
66	Holdout & Acc & d0 & d1 & d2 & d3 \\
67	 & (\%) & Rec. & Rec. & Rec. & Rec. \\
68	\midrule
69	Pythia & 62.4 & 100.0 & 49.3 & 26.8 & 73.6 \\
70	OLMo & \textbf{69.2} & 99.3 & 75.5 & 43.3 & 58.8 \\
71	GPT-2 XL & 67.6 & 98.5 & 74.7 & 52.6 & 44.5 \\
72	\midrule
73	Mean & 66.4 & 99.3 & 66.5 & 40.9 & 59.0 \\
74	\bottomrule
75	\end{tabular}
76	\end{table}
77	
78	Mean transfer accuracy is 66.4\% (2.7$\times$ chance); d0 recall ($>$98\%) inflates the headline (d1--d3 balanced mean 55.4\%).
79	
80	\subsection{Cross-Strategy Transfer}
81	\label{sec:gen:crossstrategy}
82	
83	Table~\ref{tab:cross_strategy} reports leave-one-strategy-out transfer.
84	
85	\begin{table}[t]
86	\centering
87	\small
88	\caption{Cross-strategy transfer (leave-one-out). Chance = 25\% / 33\% (d1--d3). d0 recall $\geq$89\% inflates headline; d1--d3 mean: 45.9\%.}
89	\label{tab:cross_strategy}
90	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
91	\toprule
92	Holdout & Pythia & OLMo & GPT-2 XL \\
93	 & Acc (\%) & Acc (\%) & Acc (\%) \\
94	\midrule
95	nucleus & \textbf{69.4} & \textbf{65.4} & \textbf{59.9} \\
96	temp ($\tau{=}0.9$) & 62.8 & 58.2 & 56.1 \\
97	top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) & 51.5 & 54.9 & 53.6 \\
98	\bottomrule
99	\end{tabular}
100	\end{table}
101	
102	Mean cross-strategy accuracy (59.1\%) falls 7\,pp below cross-model transfer (66.4\%); d1--d3 accuracy drops to 45.9\% (chance = 33\%).
103	The core finding is structural: training on nucleus + top-$k$ inverts the d1/d2 boundary under temperature (d1v2 AUC $<$ 0.5), because temperature scaling accelerates convergence to a low-entropy attractor (\S\ref{sec:method:theory}); depth-$d$ tail statistics under temperature therefore resemble nucleus depth-$(d{+}1)$.
104	Strategy confusion concentrates between temperature and top-$k$ (31.2\%), consistent with their opposing effects on the perplexity tail.
105	As a proof-of-concept, a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification at 57.5\% + depth classification) recovers 11.5\,pp, with a strategy-invariant floor of 67.6\% (Limitations); end-to-end PLMs lag RF by 20\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:e2e}).
106	Conditional decomposition reveals that the four-class accuracy gap between correct and wrong strategy routing is moderate ($+$4.6\,pp: 72.6\% vs.\ 68.0\%, $N{=}103{,}498$ / $76{,}502$) because d0 accuracy increases under misrouting (${\sim}$99.6\%); the d1--d3 balanced accuracy gap is 31.5\,pp (70.6\% vs.\ 39.1\%): cross-strategy difficulty is a feature-space misalignment at inter-depth boundaries, not uniform noise.
107	
108	\paragraph{Prompted generation.}
109	Replicating the GPT-2~XL nucleus pipeline with topic-seeded generation yields 69.5\% (95\% CI $[68.9, 70.2]$, $-$13.8\,pp vs.\ BOS-seeded, $2.8\times$ chance), with monotonic AUC decay and identical top features (Appendix~\ref{app:prompted_gen}): prompt conditioning attenuates but does not eliminate the depth signal.
110	
111	%% ----------------------------------------------------------------
112	\subsection{Preliminary Cross-Scale Observations}
113	\label{sec:gen:crossscale}
114	
115	Extending to 7--8B under QLoRA, Llama-3.1-8B Instruct \cite{llama3} achieves 70.2\% ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}4$) and Qwen2.5-7B \cite{qwen2.5} 60.1\% ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{>}5$).
116	At 14B (Qwen2.5-14B, self-reference model), accuracy drops to 54.1\% ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.70}{=}0$; d0v1 AUC\,=\,0.643), though d1--d3 discrimination persists (balanced accuracy 57.4\%, chance 33\%); the depth signal attenuates with scale but does not vanish (Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_full}).
117	These results are confounded by simultaneous changes in quantization (4-bit QLoRA), sample size (500 vs.\ 5{,}000), decoding strategy (nucleus only), vocabulary size, and (for 14B) reference model; they should be treated as directional evidence rather than definitive conclusions.
118	A base-model control (Llama-3.1-8B, 59.9\%, non-monotonic AUC) vs.\ instruction-tuned (70.2\%, monotonic) suggests instruction tuning \emph{regularizes} recursive degradation; a 1.5B instruct control (47.4\%, $1.9\times$ chance) confirms at matched scale (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct_1p5b}; confounds in Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_confounds}).
119	Cross-model chains (84.75\%), cross-domain (arXiv 74.1\%), and LoRA rank sensitivity ($\Delta{=}4.65$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:cross_scale_full}) further confirm robustness.

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

This paper formalizes recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and provides both theoretical grounding (\S\ref{sec:method:theory}) and empirical characterization across three 1--1.5B base model families and three decoding strategies in controlled settings.
The tail erosion mechanism and strategy-dependent convergence rates predicted in \S\ref{sec:method:theory} are confirmed across the atlas; five features suffice for 97.6\% of full performance, consistent with the low effective dimensionality of the degradation process.
Extending all three families to d4 yields 71--80\% five-class accuracy (chance = 20\%; Appendix~\ref{app:depth4_ext}); aggregate statistics (mean perplexity) saturate before tail statistics at this depth, and this saturation provides a physical explanation for the EDD ceiling.

Cross-strategy transfer is the primary bottleneck (d1--d3: 45.9\%, chance = 33\%), with d1/d2 boundary inversion under strategy mismatch revealing that different decoding strategies induce qualitatively distinct degradation trajectories; a proof-of-concept two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + depth classification) recovers 11.5\,pp.
For data curation, RF filtering (F1\,=\,0.997) outperforms perplexity thresholds (F1\,=\,0.845) for depth identification, but downstream training improvement is non-significant ($p > 0.4$; Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}, \ref{app:downstream}).
In principle, depth estimation could complement C2PA \cite{c2pa2024} and watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} by providing a retroactive, cooperation-free signal; cross-model chains (84.75\%) confirm the signal is process-level, though deployment beyond controlled settings requires addressing cross-strategy transfer.
The weakest link is d2 recall (26.8\% under cross-model transfer); BOS-seeded generation was validated under prompted conditions for only 1/9 cells ($-$13.8\,pp; \S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}).
Cross-strategy transfer and depth-quality entanglement remain open challenges (Limitations; Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}).

36	\label{app:additional}

38	\subsection{Top-$k$ Feature Trajectories}
39	\label{app:topk_trajectories}
40	
41	Figure~\ref{fig:feature_trajectory} in the main text shows feature trajectories for nucleus ($p{=}0.95$) and temperature ($\tau{=}0.9$) sampling.
42	Top-$k$ ($k{=}50$) trajectories follow the same monotonically decreasing trend for all features but with compressed inter-depth spacing, consistent with the signal attenuation effect discussed in \S\ref{sec:atlas:strategy}.
43	Concretely, the d0$\to$d1 drop in \texttt{p90\_ppl} under top-$k$ is 78\% (vs.\ 87\% for nucleus), and the d2$\to$d3 reduction is 31\% (vs.\ 39\% for nucleus).
44	Despite the magnitude reduction, feature rank ordering across depths is preserved, which explains why ordinal classifiers maintain directionality even under top-$k$ conditions.
45	
46	\subsection{Permutation Importance}
47	\label{app:permutation}
48	
49	To verify that the Gini-based importance rankings in \S\ref{sec:atlas:features} are not an artifact of the impurity measure, we compute permutation importance (5-fold CV, 10 repeats) for all 9 atlas cells.
50	The top-2 features are stable across measures: \texttt{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in 9/9 cells under both Gini and permutation importance, and \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 (vs.\ 7/9 for Gini, with the additional cell being OLMo top-$k$; the single SHAP exception is GPT-2~XL top-$k$, where \texttt{p75\_ppl} displaces \texttt{var\_surprisal} to rank 3).
51	Kendall's $W{=}0.90$ across all three methods (Gini, permutation, SHAP) indicates strong concordance ($p{<}0.005$).
52	Pairwise Spearman correlations are: SHAP--Gini $\rho{=}0.93$, SHAP--permutation $\rho{=}0.84$, Gini--permutation $\rho{=}0.76$.
53	Per-cell top-5 overlap between SHAP and permutation importance is 3--4 out of 5 features; the aggregated (mean-across-cells) top-5 sets are identical; the top features are therefore robust to the choice of importance measure at the aggregate level, though per-cell rankings exhibit model-dependent variation.

\subsection{Permutation Importance}
\label{app:permutation}

To verify that the Gini-based importance rankings in \S\ref{sec:atlas:features} are not an artifact of the impurity measure, we compute permutation importance (5-fold CV, 10 repeats) for all 9 atlas cells.
The top-2 features are stable across measures: \texttt{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in 9/9 cells under both Gini and permutation importance, and \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 (vs.\ 7/9 for Gini, with the additional cell being OLMo top-$k$; the single SHAP exception is GPT-2~XL top-$k$, where \texttt{p75\_ppl} displaces \texttt{var\_surprisal} to rank 3).
Kendall's $W{=}0.90$ across all three methods (Gini, permutation, SHAP) indicates strong concordance ($p{<}0.005$).
Pairwise Spearman correlations are: SHAP--Gini $\rho{=}0.93$, SHAP--permutation $\rho{=}0.84$, Gini--permutation $\rho{=}0.76$.
Per-cell top-5 overlap between SHAP and permutation importance is 3--4 out of 5 features; the aggregated (mean-across-cells) top-5 sets are identical; the top features are therefore robust to the choice of importance measure at the aggregate level, though per-cell rankings exhibit model-dependent variation.

\subsection{Per-Class Recall}
\label{app:per_class}

Table~\ref{tab:per_class_recall} reports per-class recall across all 9 atlas cells (4-class in-distribution, 5-fold CV).
Depth~0 recall exceeds 97\% uniformly.
Among generated depths, d2 is the hardest class in every cell; the deficit is most pronounced under top-$k$ sampling (46--53\%), where vocabulary truncation removes the tail tokens that carry depth-discriminative signal.

109	\subsection{Zero-Shot LLM Prompt Template}
110	\label{app:zeroshot_prompt}
111	
112	Both DeepSeek V3.2 and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct use identical prompting.
113	The system message defines recursive generation depth with per-depth descriptions (depth~0: human-written; depth~1--3: successive LLM generation cycles) and lists expected textual patterns at each depth (vocabulary richness, repetition, coherence).
114	The user message presents the passage (truncated to ${\approx}$384 words) and requests a JSON response containing an integer depth prediction (0--3), a confidence score, and a one-sentence reasoning.
115	No in-context examples are provided.
116	
117	\begin{quote}
118	\small
119	\textbf{System:} ``You are an expert at detecting AI-generated text and estimating its generation depth. `Recursive generation depth' refers to how many times a text has been through an LLM generation cycle: Depth~0: Original human-written text [\ldots] Depth~3: Text generated by an LLM given depth-2 text as input. Key patterns by depth: Depth~0 (human): Rich vocabulary [\ldots] Depth~3 (third-gen): Noticeable repetition, formulaic structure [\ldots]''
120	
121	\textbf{User:} ``Analyze the following text and estimate its recursive generation depth (0, 1, 2, or 3). TEXT: \{text\}. Respond with ONLY a JSON object: \{\texttt{"depth"}: $\langle$int 0--3$\rangle$, \texttt{"confidence"}: $\langle$float 0--1$\rangle$, \texttt{"reasoning"}: $\langle$str$\rangle$\}''
122	\end{quote}
123	
124	\subsection{Temperature Robustness}
125	\label{app:multi_tau}
126	
127	The cross-strategy results in \S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy} use a single temperature ($\tau{=}0.9$).
128	To test whether depth signal generalizes across temperatures, we repeat the classification pipeline at $\tau \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1\}$ on Pythia-1.4B.
129	
130	\paragraph{Within-$\tau$ robustness.}
131	For $\tau \in [0.5, 0.9]$, d1-vs-d2 AUC exceeds 0.80 (peak 0.851 at $\tau{=}0.7$, comparable to nucleus $p{=}0.95$'s 0.861) and 4-class accuracy ranges from 75.4\% to 77.3\% (Table~\ref{tab:multi_tau_within}); the depth signal is therefore not an artifact of a single temperature.
132	The same top-5 features (\texttt{var\_surprisal}, \texttt{p90\_ppl}, \texttt{mean\_ppl}, \texttt{mean\_surprisal}, \texttt{p75\_ppl}) dominate across all $\tau$ values with only minor rank-order variation.
133	
134	\paragraph{Collapse at $\tau{=}1.1$: memorization as prerequisite.}
135	At $\tau{=}1.1$, 4-class accuracy drops to 57.2\% and d1v2 AUC falls to 0.528.
136	Training loss reveals the mechanism: at low temperature ($\tau{=}0.5$), fine-tuning loss decreases steeply across recursive depths ($2.27 \to 0.42 \to 0.16$), a sign of rapid memorization of the model's own output.
137	At $\tau{=}1.1$, loss remains nearly flat ($2.27 \to 1.91 \to 1.85$); high-entropy output resists memorization, so depth-dependent distributional shifts do not accumulate.
138	This establishes \emph{memorization as a prerequisite} for detectable depth signal: recursive depth is discriminable only when successive fine-tuning iterations progressively reshape the output distribution.
139	
140	\paragraph{Cross-$\tau$ non-transferability.}
141	Leave-one-$\tau$-out transfer yields mean accuracy of 46.7\% with mean d1v2 AUC of 0.319 (Table~\ref{tab:multi_tau_cross}), worse than cross-strategy transfer (59.1\%; \S\ref{sec:gen:crossstrategy}).
142	Holdout $\tau{=}0.5$ produces inverted d1v2 AUC (0.176); different temperatures therefore produce surprisal distributions with incompatible shapes.
143	This extends the strategy-specificity finding: even within a single decoding family, the feature space is temperature-specific; strategy-conditioned classifiers are therefore necessary.
144	
145	\paragraph{Ecological validity.}
146	On WikiText-103 (546 editorial passages), all three model-specific RF classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy despite $+$621\% domain shift in mean perplexity, partly an easy case, as WikiText's higher perplexity places it farther from d1--d3 in feature space.
147	On noisier web-crawl data (5{,}000 C4 passages), FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL), concentrated in template/SEO content with high n-gram repetition (Table~\ref{tab:calibration}); deployment on heterogeneous web data requires model-specific calibration.

## Target Venue
- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main (ARR May 25, 2026)
- Backup: AAAI 2027 (abstract July 25, full paper August 1, 2026)
- EMNLP 2026 special theme "New Missions for NLP Research" explicitly calls for work on data contamination, synthetic data feedback loops, and data governance — direct venue fit

## Core Claims (3 条 + Discussion implication)

1. **Ordinal depth estimation is feasible, accurate, and robust across scales and generation modes**: Given text alone, recursive generation depth (d ∈ {0,1,2,...,K}) can be estimated with high accuracy using statistical features from reference-model perplexity distributions. On our 3-model × 3-strategy benchmark (1–1.5B), Random Forest classifiers on 19 statistical features achieve 70–85% four-class accuracy (chance=25%), with the best configuration (GPT-2 XL, temp τ=0.9) reaching 85.4%. Feature-based methods (RF, CORAL, DivEye) consistently outperform single-feature baselines across all settings. **Scale robustness**: Clean FP16 13B experiment (Qwen2.5-14B, no quantization) confirms depth signal persists at mainstream model scale, addressing the "small model only" concern from prior 7B QLoRA experiments. **Ecological validity**: Prompted generation experiment (topic-seeded text, not BOS-only unconditional) confirms depth signal is not an artifact of unnatural generation mode.

2. **Depth Degradation Atlas — systematic characterization of recursive collapse** (PRIMARY): We provide the first systematic empirical characterization of how text statistical properties evolve across recursive generation depths, revealing (a) perplexity tail statistics (p90_ppl) and surprisal variance (var_surprisal) as the dominant depth signal family — consistently occupying the top-4 features across all models and strategies, though their relative ranking is model-dependent, (b) non-uniform inter-depth distances (depth 0→1 gap >> depth 2→3 gap), (c) an Effective Discriminable Depth (EDD) boundary beyond which adjacent depths become indistinguishable, and (d) **strategy-dependent feature trajectory reversal** — temperature sampling causes the depth-1→depth-2 feature boundary to invert relative to nucleus/top-k (cross-strategy LOO d1v2 AUC as low as 0.13), demonstrating that decoding strategy fundamentally shapes the degradation trajectory rather than merely attenuating it, and (e) **accelerated convergence mechanism** — root cause analysis confirms a genuine structural distributional shift: temperature's uniform logit scaling (vs nucleus/top-k truncation) accelerates convergence to the attractor distribution, so temp09 depth N features ≈ nucleus/topk50 depth N+1 (GPT-2 XL temp09 d1 p90_ppl median=92.2, falls into nucleus/topk50 d2 range 65–92). This is not a simple scale artifact fixable by normalization — z-score normalization improves overall LR cross-strategy accuracy (25%→61%) but does **not** recover pairwise d1v2 AUC (GPT-2 XL 0.50→0.24, OLMo 0.50→0.19), and does **not** improve tree-based classifiers (RF Δ<0.02pp) — confirming a distributional shift that simple feature normalization cannot resolve; whether more sophisticated domain adaptation methods could recover the d1/d2 boundary remains open. This atlas spans 3 model families × 3 decoding strategies, with scale consistency confirmed at 14B.

3. **Cross-strategy depth estimation via two-stage pipeline + strategy-invariant signal discovery**: Naive cross-strategy transfer degrades to 59.1% with d1v2 boundary inversion. We propose a two-stage solution: (a) strategy identification classifier (57.8% — strategies share more feature space than expected), then (b) strategy-conditioned depth classifiers. The pipeline improves cross-strategy accuracy by **+11.5pp** on average (59.1% → 70.5%), with per-model results: GPT-2 XL 73.0%, OLMo 69.4%, Pythia 69.3%. Oracle ceiling at 78.3%. **Caveat**: improvement is consistent across models but absolute accuracy varies (2/3 models individually below 70%); paper must claim "+11.5pp improvement" rather than "≥70% universal recovery". The surprising finding: even with imperfect strategy routing, the pipeline works because depth signal has a **strategy-invariant core** (~60% accuracy floor) plus a strategy-specific component. This reframes cross-strategy transfer from "broken" to "substantially improved with clear ceiling for future work".

4. **[Discussion — Practical Implication]** Depth-graduated curation as alternative to binary filtering: predicted depth provides a finer-grained quality proxy than binary real/synthetic labels, enabling graduated weighting strategies. Conceptual argument supported by depth-accuracy correlation in 3×3 matrix data; full experimental validation deferred to future work (D012).

## Story Spine

- **Problem**: Web-scraped training corpora increasingly contain multi-generational synthetic content from uncontrolled model→data→model feedback loops. Existing detectors answer "is this synthetic?" but not "how many recursive cycles has this undergone?" — a critical distinction since 1st-gen synthetic data can improve training while deeply recursive text drives distribution collapse.

- **Existing approaches & gaps**: Binary detectors (LOKI, DivEye, Binoculars) classify real vs. synthetic but discard ordinal depth information. EditLens estimates single-pass AI editing extent but not recursive depth. Model collapse studies (Drayson et al. EMNLP 2025; Shumailov et al. Nature 2024) characterize degradation patterns but assume depth is known a priori — no method estimates depth from text alone.

- **Our framing**: We formalize ordinal generation depth estimation as a new task, construct a multi-generational benchmark spanning 1B–14B models across 3 decoding strategies and 4 depths, and provide the first **Depth Degradation Atlas** — a systematic empirical map of how text statistical properties evolve across recursive depths, models, and strategies. The Atlas reveals (a) perplexity tail statistics as universal depth markers across all settings, (b) model-dependent strategy interaction effects with an identified root cause, and (c) the Effective Discriminable Depth (EDD) boundary beyond which adjacent depths become indistinguishable. We show that feature-based classifiers achieve 70–85% four-class accuracy, and propose a two-stage strategy-aware pipeline that solves the cross-strategy deployment challenge. The depth signal persists under prompted generation (not just BOS-seeded), confirming ecological relevance.

- **Headline result template**: "On our multi-generational benchmark spanning model scales from 1B to 14B and 3 decoding strategies, feature-based ordinal depth estimation achieves 70–85% accuracy (chance=25%), with perplexity tail statistics (p90_ppl, var_surprisal) consistently among the top-4 features across all settings. The depth signal persists under prompted (topic-seeded) generation and at 14B scale without quantization. The Depth Degradation Atlas reveals that effective discriminable depth extends to depth 3 in 7/9 settings (T=0.75). We identify strategy-dependent feature trajectory reversal and propose a two-stage pipeline that restores near within-strategy accuracy for cross-strategy deployment."
- **Note**: 4-class (depth 0-3) is the confirmed setting. 6-class (depth 0-5) completed via plan_011.

## DCOL Status — Contingency Activated (D010/D011, 2026-05-15)

DCOL v1–v5 全部失败（embedding collapse / OOM / catastrophic forgetting / 超参违规 / NaN 梯度爆炸）。

- **Claim 2 (Atlas/EDD) 升为 PRIMARY contribution**
- **Claim 1**: Feature-based methods (RF/CORAL/DivEye) 作为 depth estimation 方法，不依赖 DCOL
- **DCOL v6 (RoBERTa-large)**: 非阻塞尝试。成功 → Section 5 bonus；失败 → negative analysis section（"contrastive ordinal learning 在文本深度估计的固有局限"）
- **Paper type**: Task formalization + systematic empirical study + practical framework（非 method paper）
- Atlas + EDD + feature universality + model-strategy interaction = 充分支撑 EMNLP "New Missions" track

## Venue Fit Risks

- **"Just an empirical study" risk**: Primary risk now that DCOL is demoted. Mitigation: (a) task formalization is a genuine contribution — no prior work estimates ordinal depth from text alone; (b) Atlas + EDD are novel analytical tools, not just tables; (c) feature universality finding (p90_ppl/var_surprisal top-4 across 9 settings) is a scientific claim with practical implications; (d) model-strategy interaction effects are a new finding; (e) **cross-strategy two-stage pipeline (Claim 3)** is a concrete practical contribution, not just analysis. EMNLP "New Missions" track explicitly values problem formalization.
- **Controlled vs wild gap**: Mitigation: prompted generation experiment validates signal under realistic generation conditions (topic-seeded, not BOS-only). Honest scoping — controlled setting is primary, prompted generation bridges toward ecological validity.
- **"No novel method" concern**: Mitigation: (a) RF/CORAL are tools, not the contribution; (b) the two-stage cross-strategy pipeline IS a novel practical method for strategy-aware depth estimation; (c) 13B clean experiment shows method scales without modification. Analogous to benchmark/analysis papers at top venues (e.g., HELM, MMLU).
- **"Small model only" concern**: Eliminated by clean 13B FP16 experiment. Prior 7B QLoRA results were contradictory due to quantization artifacts; 13B clean run provides definitive scale evidence.

## Dream-Derived Requirements (D002, 2026-05-14)

三档(best 3.0 / median 3.0 / worst 2.5)一致指出的结构性必修项：

### 论文写作硬约束
1. **DCOL loss 描述** — 若 v6 成功：Eq.1 必须包含 attractive + repulsive 双项（N-pair formulation）。若 v6 失败：negative analysis section 描述失败模式和根因分析，无需完整 loss 公式
2. **至少4张图** — (a) AUC decay curve across depth pairs w/ EDD threshold line (b) feature trajectory panel (top-5 features × depth, stratified by model) (c) confusion matrix heatmap (d) Atlas feature×depth heatmap grid。"Atlas without maps is a contradiction"
3. **Bibliography 25+ references** — 必须覆盖: watermarking (Kirchenbauer ICML 2023), model collapse theory (Alemohammad ICLR 2024, Dohmatob 2024, Gerstgrasser 2024), data curation (DSIR, QuRating), multi-source attribution (Uchendu 2020), binary detectors (Binoculars Hans ICML 2024, Fast-DetectGPT Bao 2024), decoding strategy effects (Garces Arias COLING 2025, Holtzman ICLR 2020)
4. **Surprisal reference model** — 必须明确指定 reference model、说明 cross-model LOO 时如何处理、讨论 circularity

### 指标报告硬约束

9. **"First systematic empirical map" 需限定** — Shumailov/Drayson 已有 characterization, 我们的新颖性在 ordinal estimation lens + EDD formalization + multi-model multi-strategy coverage

### Cross-Strategy 反转硬约束 (D015, Reviewer 降级条件)
10. **三档策略分类** — 论文不得将 nucleus 和 temperature 归为同一类 "soft sampling"。必须采用三档：nucleus（baseline 稳定）、temperature（信号增强但存在 d1v2 方向反转风险）、topk（信号衰减但方向一致）。D004 的 "soft sampling" 分组已被反转数据推翻。

\label{app:detector_baselines}

We evaluate whether existing binary AI-text detectors and membership inference methods, when repurposed for ordinal classification, can match our 19-feature RF pipeline.

\paragraph{Binary detectors (Pythia nucleus).}
Binoculars~\cite{binoculars2024} and Fast-DetectGPT~\cite{fast_detectgpt2024} scores are computed on the Pythia-1.4B nucleus ($p{=}0.95$) subset and fed to: (a)~a log-likelihood rank classifier (Log-Rank, 64.0\%), (b)~a combined RF trained on both detector scores (Combined, 74.2\%), and (c)~the standard 19-feature RF (78.7\%).
The 4.5\,pp gap (74.2\% vs.\ 78.7\%) confirms that perplexity distributional features capture ordinal depth structure beyond what generic detection scores provide.
Note that Fast-DetectGPT exhibits numerical overflow on Pythia nucleus d1 (mean perturbation score $>$28{,}000); results for this cell should be interpreted cautiously.
Across all 9 atlas cells, Binoculars and Fast-DetectGPT ordinal accuracy averages ${\sim}$35\% and ${\sim}$32\%, respectively.

\paragraph{Membership inference baselines (all 9 cells).}
DetectGPT~\cite{mitchell2023_detectgpt} (gpt2-large scoring model, t5-large perturbation model, 5 perturbations) achieves 30.7\% mean 4-class accuracy (d1--d3 BalAcc: 24.3\%).
Min-K\% Prob~\cite{shi2024_minkprob} ($K{=}20$) with CORAL ordinal calibration reaches 33.2\% (d1--d3 BalAcc: 40.4\%); the best single cell is gpt2xl\_temp09 at 50.6\%.
Min-K\%'s advantage over DetectGPT (+2.5\,pp) is consistent with token-level log-probabilities containing more depth-relevant information than perturbation-based curvature, but both remain within 10\,pp of chance.
CORAL calibration improves ordinal structure (d1--d3 BalAcc 40.4\% vs.\ 33.3\% random) without closing the gap to RF (71.6\%), confirming that the bottleneck is the input signal rather than the calibration strategy.
The consistent failure of all four binary/membership methods (30--35\% vs.\ RF 78.4\%) confirms that ordinal depth estimation requires depth-specific distributional features inaccessible to detection scores designed for binary classification.

\paragraph{Augmented feature set.}
To test whether detection scores carry complementary ordinal signal, we add Min-K\% probability ($K{=}20$) and DetectGPT perturbation discrepancy as additional RF features.
The 20-feature model (19 + Min-K\%) achieves 78.90\% mean 4-class accuracy (+0.48\,pp) and 72.20\% d1--d3 balanced accuracy (+0.60\,pp).
Min-K\% ranks \#3 by feature importance (0.095), behind \texttt{p90\_ppl} (0.161) and \texttt{var\_surprisal} (0.126); DetectGPT ranks \#17 (0.026).
The marginal improvement is consistent across 8 of 9 atlas cells, indicating that Min-K\%'s token-level log-probability signal provides weak but real complementary information to the passage-level distributional features.
The top-2 features (\texttt{p90\_ppl} + \texttt{var\_surprisal}) retain combined importance of 28.7\%, confirming that perplexity tail statistics remain the dominant depth markers even after augmentation.

\subsection{Prompted Generation Results}
\label{app:prompted_gen}

Table~\ref{tab:prompted_gen} reports depth estimation performance under topic-seeded (prompted) generation using GPT-2~XL with nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$, depths 0--3).
Generation is conditioned on Wikipedia topic prompts rather than a bare BOS token, a more ecologically valid test of depth signal persistence.
